author: @JBingC

text:
From what I saw, 4080 came in decently under powered compared to the XTX. 4080 also ran cooler (even before people figured out that the XTX over heated and throttled if turned on it's side). 
Overall FPS seems to be about even with the 4080, losing out in some games but overall a bit higher.
RT the 4080 beats the XTX six ways to Sunday, with the XTX barely even able to look at the last gen of cards. 
Form factor - Yup, XTX wins here, and the power adapters also fit in with more boards. Sticking to existing standards definitely makes it more user friendly.
VR: We haven't seen, but if it's like historical - buying an AMD is essentially ruining your VR experience. So if you use VR, you automatically bypass AMD even though it has more RAM. I really wish AMD would get their act together with drivers and VR. But I guess I've been waiting for AMD to get their driver issues fixed since initial Radeon days. 

All in all, $200 cheaper, but at this point (with current events), that $200 seems like a one time fee to avoid frustration with a company not backing their products, and for future annoyances trying to get things to work. Which, as I stated before - sucks. Nvidia set such a high price.. I'd have even looked at the XT if it wasn't just a broken XTX that they couldn't get working properly. If the XT was like... $500, I'd have been all over it (since it's a $400-$500 card). AMD had everything to win this time, and they blew it.

text:
This is all nice and everything, but I still do not see reasonably capable low or mid range offerings - and the thing is, I have recently bought entire and complete, including accessories, arm based miniature PC, at 25%! of a price of modern "low end" gpu offering (black Friday, true, but it is not like I saw a GPU on big promotion anywhere ever). And, to add insult to injury, integrated GPU in that ARM come with have capabilities that neither AMD nor NVidia card 25% is based of, do not posses, as those only begin to appear in GPU models at least twice the price, and then come with additional downsides (power requirements, size, noise) aside of price.

As I see it, GPU market currently is classic "frog in a well" scenario with PC/GPU manufacturers, companies that were already living in their own little worlds, derailing completely during crypto gold-rush. Highly competitive ARM market is stepping on their feet capability wise, taking over young generations (future high-end users!) like a storm, offering "real" operating systems and tools (linux, mac ARM offerings), taking first steps in high performance markets with Apple M1 chips, even scalability in case of some board solutions.

What benefits remain limited to x86 PC domain?
Upgradebility? Not really, if there is no one willing to manufacture and sell actual upgrades...
Computation? You mean specifically cryptomining? Because actual computation is a whirlwind of new/modified ideas and tools, requiring both healthy user and developer communities, communities that are currently disintegrating due to PC & GPU manufacturers forcing choices most beneficial to themselves onto customers, regardless how far from actual demand their are. This is "no real competition Intel" all over again, this time on 2 producers.
What other benefits are there? Inertia is not something that can get you very far, and may I remind that reasonably priced competently designed solutions taking over "undisputed kings" once they went too far in their profit margin pursuits and "visions" is basically a title of industry theme-song in general, personal computing specifically...

Producer of the ARM mini-computer have new, more powerful models in their roadmap (using already existing hardware), that offer enough benefits for me to justify migration (not just standard use but also development), benefits NVidia already cannot compete with, and AMD will loose as soon as I'm done migrating, because catching up is not enough once the barrier of entry acts in your disfavor. 

This post is not an appeal, since light has already established itself on a horizon in form of a real competition but a voice of reason in favor of (currently in theory only) better solution PC modular by design concept and standardization is in general.

text:
Here is why I went AMD..

I was thrilled to pick up a new AMD 6900xt Reference card for $700 on eBay back in October after waiting so long for prices to start to even out. I was coming from an Nvidia 1060 6GB with an Intel I5 that to this day can still hold it's ground and has plenty of life left for 1080p gaming (And also for Sale as a complete PC on eBay for anyone who is interested) , that thing was some of the best bang for you buck I've had! Safe to say I am very happy with my 6900xt, I didn't like the direction Nvidia was taking, and I always saw AMD as the "Android" and Nvidia as the "iPhone" but this generation gives me all the faith in AMD, their Processors are fantastic, and my GPU has been a monster! What intrigued me as as someone who enjoys their fair share of games of all types was their Smart Access Memory Technology, and the fact that AMD's GPU's seemed to be very underrepresented in the PC community. I looked at their catalogue of what they have to offer, and what I liked was the look of their lineup - it's simple, bold, and looks like it knows how to party when needed, and be also be all business. There is no denying that Nvidia is a leader in some categories like Ray Tracing being vastly superior, and 4k gaming, along with being easier to use with other software and such for developers. But NVidias offerings also cost more, and consume more power along with their GPU's being larger in size and frankly Uglier (although you have a TON of other manufacturer options so that's also a huge plus) What made me choose AMD was it's value per dollar. Let's be honest, most of us aren't buying super top end space ships for our PC's (I paired my 6900xt with a Ryzen 5 5600x) which is why AMD got my dollar. I find it more important now than ever to vote with your money. Nvidia and Intel have been absolutely CHECKED by AMD, and rightfully so. I'm someone who isn't loyal to a brand name, and who loves games from all systems. I just want my hard earned money to go to the product that fits my needs most for a reasonable price, and AMD has done that. Most of you aren't here for benchmarks and all that stuff, and I feel like too much of the PC gaming community invests too much time comparing specs, brands, and framerates instead of just enjoying your games. Don't get me wrong, I love me some specs, and silky smooth framerates but I care most about the experience. For that my 6900xt has given me a very rich experience with everything I've thrown at it. The only thing I'd really be able to notice with my eyes is the Ray Tracing being a little rough compared to Nvidia, but I honestly don't use the Ray Tracing option. I play my games on my 2k monitor, and I've been absolutely delighted. I like AMD's Adrenalin software and have had nothing but a breezy, smooth, strong experience. I love that my GPU is more energy efficient, smaller in size, and provides everything I want, and then some for a better price than Nvidias offerings do. Nvidia and AMD are keeping each other competitive and we all benefit from it! But AMD performs better per dollar and watts than Nvidia does. Nvidia can rev their engine a little higher, but 99% of you would not be able to notice with your naked eye nor even have the hardware to fully utilize the difference in higher end power. As of right now AMD has shown me they care about the value and performance to their customers, and look like they are continuing to do so, and for that I am team AMD at the moment =)

text:
The whole stigma around AMD drivers is really over-blown. I have run Radeon cards since the 9800 Pro (including the x1900XTX from which this card's namesake was derived) and I've not run into any issues I didn't also encounter on nVidia cards. That script flips when you try to use nVidia on linux, where the lack of proper driver support really shows and Radeon routinely outperforms nVidia.

The encoder also isn't as bad as people make out - it just isn't on par with nvenc at the same bitrate (meaning you just need to use a higher bitrate and suffer slightly larger file sizes). Like they said in the video, hopefully AV1 takes over and this will all start to standardize a bit.

I feel a more valid point of criticism is that professional applications don't leverage OpenCL to the same degree as Cuda. Hopefully AMD starts making some in-roads towards resolving that with this generation.

text: Actually, AMD's HEVC has always been vastly superior to NVidia's NVENC (and NVENC actually became decent just a couple of years ago). The problem is - or, was, if PR releases are to be believed - that streaming softwares like OBS didn't support AMD's HEVC (because >market share, and that's understandable. Also AMD's software became good only in 2020 - NVidia's software is still bad, meanwhile) and so AMD users were forced to use AMD's AVC encoder which is pretty awful. Right now the golden standard for GPU encoding is still AMD's HEVC, and will probably still be so for 1-2 years, since psy optimizations on AV1 are not on par.

I love this entire tech arc these last few years.

AMD was seen coming by Intel.
They ignored it.
They were sent a threat that AMD is coming.
Intel kept ignoring it.
AMD used the fact that Intel flat out lied to consumers for years about what was affordable for consumer grade multi core processors to climb to the top.
AMD proceeded to tell Nvidia that they are coming.
Nvidia ignored it.
AMD released something pretty great for Radeon with their Rx series, Nvidia was just happy flexing with raw power because they're still better, crapping on consumers by skyrocketing prices.
AMD kept improving.  Nvidia took it seriously by offering their next gen for the same msrp (miners got in our way again).  
AMD reenacting the Rocky movies where some nobody comes out of the blue with a title shot and makes enough ruckus that they get a rematch and proceed to win.
And they're getting ready to do it again.

All the while us consumers are loving AMD.  In spite of us knowing that they want to make money.  Because they're keeping the giants honest.  Even if they're willing to make the easy money where they can, they're not letting Intel and Nvidia lie to us for over a decade anymore.

text: @GruntyGame  Amd lost it's market share by constantly abandoning runtimes and hardware. Hip 2 is the current AMD library, and less than 8 AMD cards ever made can run it. Meanwhile Nvidia still uses CUDA. CUDA has a 15+ year history of development. Nvidia has released literally hundreds of different models that are mostly backwards CUDA compatible. AMD did this to themselves without anyone else's help. Developers are hesitant to adopt a runtime from a manufacturer that has a history of complete abandonment of their own products and partners. Which is why very few companies write programs specifically for AMD hardware. AMD is currently at 10% of the discrete gpu market based on a November 2022 report, and the trend is continuing down for that very reason. Why would anyone buy this or the next generation of cards when it has already been hinted at that RNDA will be replaced by Instinct. Will instinct abandon prior hardware for a new runtime again? De ja vu......... AMD is sort of like buying a cheap car just to occupy a parking space..... Sure you can drive it once in a while on rarely used back roads and have a blast, but you can never drive it on the Cuda or Optix expressways virtually every developer uses, including many game developers..... And don't tell me that only 1% of users use CUDA, because that is complete AMD crowd hyped BS.... Windows knows how to use CUDA right out of the box and has since Vista SP1 in 2007....  Oddly enough, the AMD gaming arena thinks that AMD will somehow miraculously make a comeback and dominate Nvidia. Which is very odd, because that would mean thousands of developers would have to help them do it and risk abandonment, again. I don't see that ever happening unless Nvidia stops making gpus altogether. Then AMD probably still wont make it to the top if that happens due to practices the majority of the industry is well aware of, from past and present experiences..

text:
As far as I understand, the functions of memory cache dies do shrink well at least i would say so. (Maybe Linus is just using “shrink well” differently from how i would) but the benefits of shrinking them aren’t there. They could make them a smaller more efficient die but after the cost of porting the tech to a new process and additional cost of that new process, and the fact that the process is less refined than 6nm, any yield benefits from having a smaller die are negligible and the memory isn’t exactly the primary source of power draw so they don’t really need to worry as much about efficiency.
Also I’m excited to see the AIB cards. Efficiency is great and for daily driving, I prefer undervolting rather than overclocking but I do like overclocking so it’ll be cool to see how fast you can get those AIB cards with another 35W or so.

author: @MrMeerkat818

text: @Steve Sherman Technically they can. If you're talking watts, that single 12VHPWR cable can provide 600W on its own. It's kind of the whole point of moving to it as a standard. Less cables/cable clutter, and only one cable needed to do the same job we've been using three cables to do. That also means that should a card need anything between 601W and 1200W, they only need one more connector. The number of connectors would be getting way out of hand if you were to keep using the traditional 8-pin PCIe cable. But point being the 4090 is 450W, and it's been shown that you can undervolt it and lose very little in performance. So not only does NVIDIA still have 150W to work with, but further optimizations could make that need a bit lower with no performance loss.

@SupraSav  These people make money putting out videos.

If they don't get the video out right as embargo lifts, and someone else does, they don't make money.

LTT aren't going to go broke missing 1 deadline, but a lot of the smaller techtubers literally don't get paid if they don't get the video out quickly enough.  "They still make the video why wont they get paid?"  because you get paid based on views, and your views absolutely SUCK if you don't get it out quickly.

GPU vendors sending cards for testing before embargo release date let these people do the testing in a reasonalbe time frame, this ensures the numbers they give us are good quality tests.  Sending out cards with no time to test results in BAD information for us, (literally wrong information) because they do these tests in a hurry, because if they don't get it out quickly - welp, who needs to eat this week?

I have heard some techtubers talk about big-name product launches being the way they literally pay for a quarter of the years worth of content they produce.

So if you like a smaller youtuber that does reviews on products you actually want (rather than just the big name reviews they also do), then you want them to get their big-name review out ASAP (and not crunch it) so they can pay for their smaller niche content.

text:
05:45  No it doesn't.  It has 20% more stream processors.  But with RDNA 3, each stream processor can do one FP32 and one INT32, or two FP32.  Same as Ampere and Lovelace.  The difference is that AMD isn't dishonestly inflating the advertised number of stream processors, while nVidia is lying about the CUDA core count (i.e. the 4090 has 8192 CUDA cores, not 16384).

Just as with Ampere and Lovelace, RDNA 3 will not be able to actually utilize all that FP32 capacity in games.  nVidia achieves about 25% of the extra compute on average at 4K.  The easiest way to see that is to compare the performance of the 2080 Ti and the 3080, which have the same clock speeds and same CUDA core counts.  The difference is that the 3080 has the dual-FP32 capability.  AMD's performance numbers are in line with similar results for RDNA 3.  So when comparing the 7900 XTX to the 6950 XT, it's basically comparing an effective shader count of 7680 to 5120.  Given the similar clock speeds, that lines up with a typical performance uplift of about 50%.

text: It's not anything like Ryzen. All compute is on one big die, it functions just like monolithic design. Chiplets are just moving cache, memory controllers and memory interface off expensive 5nm, this stuff doesn't scale well with node advances.
author: @kognak6640

text: @kognak6640  yeah but it’s all operating off interconnects. They claim they fix this with clocks. Idk about that so far only massive amounts of cache can remedy that.
author: @unicornharry7995

text:
@unicornharry7995  You still pulling from Ryzens. It doesn't apply because GPUs do not work like CPUs. GPUs need bandwidth, not latency. That's why GDDR has terrible latency but very high bandwidth.
Also on RDNA3 the big cache is behind the interconnects, not in front like CPUs. It's obviously there not to "remedy" supposed interconnect weakness. On Ryzen big cache in center, surrounded by cores for lowest possible latency. On RDNA2 big cache is on edges to increase effective bandwidth, it's not latency optimized at all. And now just moved on separated chips. Interconnects themselves are very high bandwidth busses, multiple times faster than two GDDR6 chips per MCD provides.

text:
@Random_dud31  it can depend on the game, ray tracing in a game like hitman is groundbreakingly beautiful but also functional. Being able to see movement in a reflection or a shadow of a character model that is off screen is massive, however I do hope that developers don't go all in on raytracing yet.

As good looking as it is, making games have functionally beautiful reflection and shadow maps with the work arounds we've been using (and even making those methods work better) should still be a focus. Raytracing can look really good and it's actually relatively hands off for game devs to add to the game (compared to SSR and shadow mapping). One day we can start releasing games where non-ray tracing cards will just... have no shadows or reflections, but we're definitely not there, but sadly there are games that have gone this approach (one such game doesn't even launch without an "RTX" capable card).

The problem with RTX, and why it's really hard to justify the framerate hit for most people, is the fact that we have "good enough" solutions that have been in games since quake 2 and most game devs work on making it better and better. The crux is it takes a lot of effort, since it's "fake" shadows and reflections, there's a lot of limitations and loss in quality and accuracy and an increase in the time developers spend on it. Meanwhile ray tracing just auto solves shadows and reflections, sure the model makers (and texture artists) have to spend a bit of effort for enabling ray tracing to work, but they no longer have to build a fake shader. What is happening though is kinda the worst of both worlds, as ray tracing is more and more possible, devs are spending less and less time working on the "fake" shadows and reflection systems and putting their beans in the ray tracing pot. Cyberpunk has amazing looking shadows and reflections (plus the light refractions) but if you don't have ray tracing a lot of objects just don't cast shadows, mirrors don't even have a reflection unless you "activate" them... it's almost like they used ray tracing to cut corners, not to make it look better.

So what we get is a game with shadows and lighting that's only really a step above PS2 global emission unless you click on ray tracing. For most people that's plenty good enough, it has fake shadows in enough places to feel "lit" the most people ignore the lack of reflections in the puddles and only think about reflections when it comes to mirrors. They're "good enough" for people, but relatively terrible compared to the ray traced solutions.

In plenty of games I feel like ray tracing isn't necessary because the developer (like hitman 3 from my earlier example) spent plenty of time making a robust and good looking game without the need for ray tracing. I still like that they add the support (that's how we drive demand for cards) but I'm not a fan of the trend of having ray tracing replace traditional fake lighting/reflection.

text:
AMD???

AMD is going to get pushed out of the market by Intel if anything because Intel already understands AI in a GPU.  Intel also already understands tile based circuits and 14th gen is tile based.

In the mean time AMD is about to put out GPUs where their drivers still aren't ready, something Nvidia hasn't done in many years.  Nvidia, even with a 4080 not selling very well can easily adjust pricing and still make a decent profit margin.  And it's not AMD forcing Nvidia to do anything, it's the consumer.  Most people want AMD to succeed to bring down pricing on Nvidia GPUs so they can buy an Nvidia GPU.  That doesn't do anyone any good.  AMD still only sells about 10% of graphics cards, while Nvidia owns the other 90%, and what Intel is eating into is AMD sales.

It's STILL the perception among the wealthy buyers (about 20% of wealthy country households) that don't spend all day watching Youtube videos that Nvidia is the high quality product that you buy and it works and it doesn't give your system any problems.  AMD is still perceived to be the budget product because it's not as good of quality.  And if AMD releases RDNA 3 with driver issues and it looks like they will, it reinforces this perception.  And this is why AMD's best selling GPUs for RDNA 2 are often an AIB variant of a 6600, and on the other hand Nvidia can have a best selling AIB variant that's a 3090 Ti and the 4090 doesn't stay in stock.  AMD makes an excellent product with the 6800 XT.  It's rare that anything above a 6700 XT is in Amazon's top 50 best selling GPUs.  It's rare that AMD AIB GPUs are even in Amazon's top 50 best selling GPUs.  Sometimes there's only 3 or 4 AMD products in that list.  Their prices have been climbing back up along with Nvidia in the last 2 - 3 weeks, and when that happens Nvidia dominates that top 50 list.

So yes, Nvidia can't do whatever they want, but it's not because of AMD, it's because of consumers choosing which Nvidia GPU they're going to buy.
